system:
You are a medicinal chemist advising a hit-to-lead optimisation campaign.

You will be shown compounds from a congeneric series with their measured
potencies, and a numbered menu of substructures that occur in the virtual
library. Your job is to state a structural hypothesis about what makes a
compound potent in this series, as a constraint that will narrow the library.

You choose substructures by their menu index. You do not write SMARTS.

Guidance:
- Aim to keep roughly 5-25% of the library. Each menu entry shows how much of
  the library it matches; requiring two entries keeps at most the smaller.
- Prefer one or two well-chosen entries. Requiring many at once usually matches
  nothing, which wastes the constraint entirely.
- Only state a descriptor range if the data supports it. Use a wide range when
  you mean "unbounded on this side".
- You are choosing what to *explore*, not predicting individual values. A
  constraint that excludes the best compound is far worse than one that is
  slightly too permissive.

Respond with JSON only.

response.hypothesis: The most potent compounds in this series appear to share a specific core scaffold containing a fused bicyclic aromatic system with a specific substitution pattern, rather than just generic amide or fluorine features. Compounds 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 (pchembl > 7.3) all contain the motif c1ccc(Nc2ncnc3ccccc23)cc1 (or very similar fused systems), whereas the lower potency compounds (6-10) lack this specific core or have significantly altered scaffolds (e.g., simple phenyls, sulfones, or different heterocycles). While substructure [4] matches 532 compounds (25.5%), it is the only one that captures the high-potency cluster. Substructure [7] (fused bicyclic aromatic) matches 215 compounds (10.3%) and likely refines this further by excluding simple phenyls or non-fused systems present in the lower potency hits like compound 6 or 9. Combining [4] and [7] would be too restrictive (likely <1% of library), so focusing on the core scaffold [4] is the primary filter, potentially augmented by [7] if the library size allows, but [4] alone is the strongest predictor based on the data provided.
